topic: Agent Trajectory: Terminal Monitor for AI Coding Agents

key_points: An AI coding agent dashboard should answer four questions fast: which agents are running, which one needs input, which checkout each agent owns, and can you respond without finding the original terminal
The category is really four product shapes and comparing them as interchangeable produces a misleading checklist: tmux sidebar/TUI, browser dashboard, native desktop app, and mobile companion/PWA
'Worktree automation and dashboard coverage are separate decisions' — a tool can own worktree lifecycle or merely discover existing tmux panes; neither model is inherently better
Compared dmux, workmux, webmux, AgentDock, Agent of Empires, ClawTab across tmux relationship, worktrees, agent state, phone path, and recovery/scheduling (checked 2026-08-14)
Agent state vocabulary in practice: working, asking, idle, error, approvals, tool state, and first/latest query
Coding-agent observability is its own category: agents plan, edit files, run shell commands, call subagents and write to git under one user task, so failures are per-session, not per-tool

Canonical failure modes invisible on per-tool dashboards: wrong tool name passed three times before a hallucinated stack trace, a 4,200-token edit on a file that needed three lines, a failing shell command silently retried seven times

Per-agent OTel surface as of Aug 2026: Claude Code 1.0 GA (2026-06-26) native hook spans on PreToolUse/PostToolUse/SubagentStart/SubagentStop with gen_ai.* attributes and 8 KB tool-output truncation; Gemini CLI GA (2026-06-15) --telemetry-otlp-endpoint using OpenInference (needs attribute rename); Codex CLI --otel-endpoint; OpenCode v0.4.0 --analytics-config with opencode.cost.session_total; GitHub Copilot Chat org-token-only spans lacking tool sub-attributes; AWS Kiro preview with prompt-template IDs
Only Codex CLI emits coding_agent.tool_call.duration_ms directly — elsewhere you compute duration from span start/end
Proposes a normalized schema putting all six streams on one timeline plus a five-panel view (latency, retries, file-edit shape, subagent call depth, prompt-supply-chain)

AgentPulse (MIT, by Conal Hickey) reads Claude Code, Cursor and Codex transcripts and assigns one of six states: converging, exploring, stuck, done, drifting, idle — with no model call, no telemetry, no network

Default analysis window is 20 minutes; the live TUI refreshes every 30 seconds, drops sessions after one hour idle, and shows up to 10 sessions; `npx @conalh/agentpulse@latest live` opens a terminal dashboard rather than a hosted control plane
--strict exits 1 when a session is drifting or stuck; --fail-on-error is a separate gate for unreadable transcripts; the bundled GitHub Action enables it by default

'Drifting' is deliberately narrow: privileged paths (.ssh, .aws, .kube, /etc/shadow), a curl/wget piped into sh/bash/zsh, or a Write/Edit outside the repo root — and it explicitly does not cover process substitution, download-then-execute chains, package install hooks, or symlink escapes

Core argument: a trajectory label is not a quality score; deterministic rules miss behavior outside their vocabulary but are reproducible, and blind spots should be visible (cf. NIST 'not addressed' vs 'silently passed')
Local analysis can still leak through CI: derived labels, verdicts, narratives and topic keywords can reach step summaries or PR comments; recommends redact: all when sensitive
Commercial framing: 'Agent Trajectory Monitors' alert on agent span occurrence and relationship patterns using Monitors as Code
Trajectory monitoring is positioned as the evolution of span-level monitoring: not whether one span is slow, but whether spans occur and relate as they should
Sits inside a broader agent-observability suite (trace/conversation structure, conversation clusters, agent evaluation, metric and validation monitors)

On 2026-07-20 OpenAI described failures from a long-running internal model that existing deployment evaluations missed: separate actions looked acceptable while their combined purpose bypassed a control — access was paused and monitoring added that evaluates the evolving trajectory
Google DeepMind's analysis of one million agent tasks found most flagged events came from misinterpretation or overeagerness, not hostile intent

Per-action controls (validate arguments, enforce permissions, require approval) answer 'is one operation allowed now'; trajectory monitoring answers 'given everything already attempted, what is this run trying to accomplish now?'
Six-moment monitor card: goal accepted, plan changed, tool selected, result observed, boundary reached, completion claimed — each with a high-signal warning and a default response

Build the monitor on observable evidence, not generated reasoning: models may omit, summarize poorly, or explain behavior they did not perform; turn the request into invariants before the first consequential tool call
Evaluates six terminals specifically for AI-coding workloads (MOLTamp, Warp, Wave Terminal, Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2), explicitly favoring observability into agent activity over raw speed

Describes the AI-coding terminal workload: long sessions, a token counter to catch an agent going off the rails, hook events firing on tool calls, rerunning the same command thirty times until the diff is right
MOLTamp's differentiator is a hook event stream plus token counter and skins tuned for agent output, wrapping Claude Code/Codex/Gemini/Aider rather than replacing them

Argues 'best agent terminal' has no single answer because three questions belong to three layers: does it render an agent TUI correctly (multi-line input, notifications, Unicode, scrollback while the alt screen is owned), does the session outlive you, and can you see which agent is stuck
Names the expensive failure explicitly: an agent sitting blocked on a permission prompt for forty minutes across six agents in three repos
Positions Herdr as a runtime that keeps many agents alive and reports which one is blocked; emulators (Ghostty, iTerm2, Kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty) as rendering surface only
'Agent Deck' — a rich terminal dashboard for monitoring and controlling multiple AI coding agent sessions (Rust, MIT, 108 stars as of 2026-10-01, active same-day)
Install path is brew/nix plus `dot-agent-deck hooks install`, then `dot-agent-deck`; the hook install is what feeds the dashboard
Docs are published agent-first (llms.txt index), i.e. the monitor expects an agent to configure it
c9watch (claude code watch) is a macOS desktop dashboard over every Claude Code, Codex and Cursor Agent session on the machine, plus a JSON CLI for agents (Rust, MIT, 128 stars)
Key design choice: it discovers sessions by scanning running processes at the OS level, so you can start an agent from any terminal or IDE — no plugins, no workflow change, no vendor lock-in
States surfaced: which agent needs permission, which is working, which is idle — and agents can query the same session status to coordinate with each other

PI Dashboard: real-time web dashboard for pi coding-agent sessions with multi-session view, live chat mirroring, integrated terminal, diff viewer and mobile-first remote control (TypeScript, MIT, 308 stars)
Coexists with pi's TUI rather than replacing it; remote access via mDNS or zrok tunnel
Shows the vendor-lock pole of the category — it works only with the pi agent — versus c9watch's discovery-based neutrality
Sidekick Agent Hub: a full TUI dashboard tracking tokens, cost and context across Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex, shipped as a VS Code extension and CLI (TypeScript, MIT, 85 stars)
Bundles inline completions and code transforms alongside monitoring, plus switching between multiple Claude Code and Codex accounts
Representative of the 'monitor plus productivity harness' bundle that the pure-monitor tools deliberately avoid

SOURCE FETCH BLOCKED (curl failed; recorded as unavailable per research policy) — only the indexed description is verified: 'When you had one Claude Code session open, you could watch the diffs scroll by. The moment you fan out into parallel agents, each editing its own corner of the repo, the terminal becomes a wall of overlapping output'
Cited for the 'wall of overlapping output' framing of the multi-agent monitoring problem; do not attribute specific tool claims to this source without re-fetching

stats.fact: Production-scale agentic coding workload characterization: 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls and 95T tokens (sampled GitHub Copilot traces, June 2026) — sessions are sparse user-initiated turns, each unfolding into an autonomous agent loop almost always coupled with tool execution
stats.source: arXiv:2608.00101 'Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale' (2026-07-30)

stats.fact: KV cache hit rate averages ~90% within a turn but falls to ~55% across turn boundaries and is drastically invalidated by model switches or context compaction — a concrete reason a monitor can see and predict waste that a per-call view cannot
A lightweight idle-time predictor captures 86-90% of total idle time, highlighting minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries against quick agentic turnaround

In a randomized controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% SLOWER with early-2025 AI coding tools, while believing they had been sped up by ~20% — the perception gap is the argument for instrumenting the trajectory instead of trusting the vibe
stats.source: METR, 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity' (arXiv:2507.09089; last verified 2026-09-11)

stats.fact: Agent usage at work nearly doubled year over year (31% -> 59%) across 1,100 developers and professionals; 60% block agents from making unapproved system changes and 68% prefer predictable single-agent setups over multi-agent configurations
stats.source: Stack Overflow pulse survey, 'Agents on a leash' (2026-05-27)

stats.fact: 63% of technologists rarely or never let agents run entirely on autopilot, and humans remain in the loop — i.e. the monitor's job is attention routing, not full automation

Claude Code 1.0 GA (2026-06-26) ships native OpenTelemetry hook spans on every PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SubagentStart and SubagentStop with gen_ai.* attributes by default, tool output truncated to 8 KB; opt-in via OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
stats.source: Stack Pulsar, 'AI Coding Agent Observability 2026: Six Tools' (2026-08-13), verified against upstream docs

stats.fact: Cross-agent dashboards break on attribute drift: Gemini CLI and Codex CLI emit OpenInference attribute names rather than gen_ai.*, requiring a collector attribute-rename processor before they share one timeline with Claude Code or OpenCode
Gartner puts LLM-observability adoption at roughly 15% of enterprise GenAI deployments (up from ~5% a year earlier), projected to reach 50% by 2028
stats.source: codewithrashid.com, 'Your Agent Is Already in Production' (secondary citation of Gartner — treat as indicative, not primary)

stats.fact: LivePlan decouples judging from advising: a deterministic rule-based monitor inspects trajectory signals without invoking an LLM, and only on detection consults an advisor LLM for a high-level next-step correction — avoiding misleading global re-planning
stats.source: arXiv:2608.06701 'Online Monitoring and Corrective Steering of Programming Agents' (2026-08-07)

stats.fact: Agent Trajectory Sentinel is a one-class behavioural monitor trained on healthy runs only: ~219 microseconds per step, 3.95 MB of state, no model internals read (telemetry only), refits in 1.7 s versus 68 s for a GRU, with 2,823 committed traces

A developer running 3-6 CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, Aider) across git worktrees on a 300k-line monorepo reports the throughput is great but managing it is not: agents sit waiting for a file-write permission in a tab you forgot existed
stats.source: Hacker News story 47268777, 'Is anyone else drowning in terminal tabs running AI coding agents?' (author comment)

stats.fact: The 2026 CLI coding-agent ecosystem is large enough to index: a curated directory lists 130+ terminal-native CLI coding agents plus their harnesses (last updated 2026-09-28)

angles: Layer, not brand: the terminal question is really three layers — emulator (renders the agent TUI), runtime/multiplexer (keeps sessions alive and reports which one is blocked), and trajectory monitor (compresses many agents into one attention queue). A review that picks by layer ages better than a top-5 list.

The wedge is the permission prompt, but the value is the trajectory: every tool in this category started by answering 'which agent is stuck?' — the deeper layer is whether the sequence of tool calls is still pointed at the authorized goal (AgentKit's six-moment card, LivePlan's drift detection).

Deterministic local rules vs LLM judges is the real 2026 split: AgentPulse and LivePlan both refuse to let a second model judge the first. That buys reproducibility, zero network and ~200us/step decisions, at the cost of blind spots — and a credible review says which blind spots rather than hiding them.

Read the trajectory, not the transcript: models omit or mis-summarize their own reasoning, so a monitor must be built on observable evidence (tool names, normalized args, file edits, retries, context-window occupancy, exit codes) rather than on generated rationales.

Native OTel hooks changed the plumbing: you no longer have to scrape JSONL if the agent emits gen_ai.* spans — but attribute drift (gen_ai.* vs OpenInference) silently fragments cross-agent dashboards, so normalization belongs in the collector, not the tool.

What a per-tool dashboard cannot show: three wrong tool names before a hallucinated stack trace, a 4,200-token edit that should have been three lines, a shell command silently retried seven times. Per-session traces are the only surface where those appear.

Local-first has a leak channel: 'no network' describes the runtime, not the workflow — transcript-derived labels, verdicts, narratives and topic keywords can reach CI step summaries and PR comments. Path redaction only reduces exposure.

Monitor the monitor: METR's 19% slowdown with a 20% perceived speedup is the strongest argument that agent productivity cannot be self-reported — trajectory data is the only honest scoreboard, including for the monitoring tool itself.

Neutral discovery vs vendor lock is a buying axis: c9watch scans running processes so any terminal/IDE works, while PI Dashboard works only with pi and OctoAlly wants you to launch from it. Review should state which model fits an existing workflow.
